questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose James Cook University (JCU) due to its expertise in Marine Biology, which I’m very interested in, and then I also really wanted to travel in Australia.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy. However, it was a bit confusing to know whether I had done everything that I needed to do, or if I had overlooked something. Would have been nice with some sort of check list.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I emailed a bit with the inquiry email available at JCU about my courses. Other than that they gave us an online introduction meeting and a presentation of the uni at orientation week.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: There could have been more arranged for the international students when we arrived at the uni. E.g. more social events to help us meet new people. There was only one day that was fully planned for us, and the rest of the week it was a bit hard to figure out how to meet new people. I heard from previous students that there used to be more set up by the uni, and that would have been nice.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There was Burralga Yumba, Rotary International House, George Roberts, John Flynn College, and the Saints College.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: I lived at Rotary International house. There was no meal plan set, and you were responsiple for your own food and cooking. At Rotary you share an apartment with 7 other people, who you share a kitchen with. In the kitchen you'll bind all of the necessary facilities and equipment for cooking.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Burralga Yumba (BY) and Rotary International House (Rotary) are the two most popular options. They are also two very different places to live, however. I lived at Rotary. Here you share an apartment with 6 other people, and this suited me very well. We became very close friends and had a great community together. There was also a great social community between the different apartments at Rotary, and we did many things together - Movie nights, swimming at the lagoon or pontoon, trips to Magnetic Island or other places, and big communal dinners with up to 25 people attending! However, this also only happened because we made an effort for it to happen. At Rotary there aren’t as many events planned for you by the campus housing as there are at BY. Therefore, I don’t think it necessarily always is this social at Rotary, but if you put your time and effort into it, then it can happen, and for me it was definitely worth it! BY is also a great place to live I think (and know from friends). However, it’s a much bigger place with 400 students living there and sharing all the same (giant) kitchen and common areas. A lot of things were going on at BY, and we came there for parties and other social events, which was great! However, friends who lived there told me, that it could also be a bit chaotic living there, and that it was just too many people living there, for there to really be a close and tight community like the ones we had in our apartments at Rotary. However, you perhaps also have to be luckier with who you live with in the apartment at Rotary, whereas at BY you aren’t as dependent on that because you’ll always be able to find some people that you like in such a big crowd. All in all, I think both places are great places to live, and In both cases, it is really also just what you make of it. Try your best to invest yourself in the social community, and don’t be shy to invite people to do things! Everyone is looking for new friends, things to do and people to explore the area with. It’s great living on campus, and I would definitely recommend this instead of living off campus - even though this might be cheaper. You get so much social given to you, and this is just so important (especially in the beginning) when you move to a new place where you don’t know anyone. I know from friends who lived off campus, that they regretted it.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: When you get the confirmation from KU that you have been admitted, you'll need to wait for JCU to allow you to apply for the confirmation of enrollment (COE). This may take some time. Hereafter, you'll fill out a lot of paperwork to get the COE, and your payment for the tuition fee needs to go through. This may also take some time.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I only emailed a bit with the enquiri email at JCU to get information about the students health care (you'll need one that is partner with JCU, and you therefore can't just use your own from e.g. your travle ensurrance.)

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes that I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The registration process takes quite a lot of time and is a bit confusing - Don’t lose patients, because it is definitely worth it.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The level of the course wasn’t necessarily higher, but it might sometimes be assumed that you have some knowledge that you don’t have. For example, I had Coral reef ecology, and in this course, it was assumed that you knew the basic biology of a coral, which I didn’t, and I therefore had to do a bit of extra work in the beginning, but after that it was fine. In many of my classes it was also assumed that you knew basic statistics and could work in the program R. Even though I had a course in this at KU in Denmark, I had forgotten a lot of it, and I would therefore recommend doing a little brush-up on beforehand. They were however also very helpful with assisting you, and I became much more confident in using the program afterwards, so you’ll also be fine without the brush-up. 

I would say the level of the exams was pretty much the same as back home.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I would say the quality of education is very high at JCU - especially if you are doing courses in marine science. The style of teaching is a bit different than at KU, since you have a lot more assignments. This was a bit stressful, but also kind of nice, because then your grade isn’t just based on one exam. To begin with, it was also difficult for me to do the assignments, since most of them had to be written as scientific articles where you had to find your own literature, and I just hadn’t really had that much experience with this a my home university. So, this was definitely a challenge to begin with, but it actually ended up being a quite nice way of learning, and I really learned a lot from it.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Coral reef ecology - MB3190
Geographical Information Systems (GIS) - EV2502
Inductory marine science - MB1110
Marine conservation biology - MB3200

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would in particular recommend Coral reef Ecology and Marine Conservation Biology (if you are interested in marine biology). The professors teaching these courses are extremely competent and on top of their research field. The material is also very new and relevant, which makes the content even more exciting. In Coral reef ecology you’ll also go on a field trip, where you collect your own data while diving/snorkeling, and afterward, you’ll analyze the data and write a scientific report. The trip in itself is a lot of fun. People are very friendly, and you get to go snorkeling and see coral reefs during your time studying! You’ll also just learn a lot from the entire trip, and I thought It also was very nice getting some experience with some hands-on practical work since the bachelor in biology at KU isn’t that practical. 

Inductory marine science was alright, but it was a 1st year subject, and it tried to cover a lot of content. However, it was all quite superficial, and therefore some of the things were kind of hard to remember, and i therefore actually found it a bit difficult to prepare for at the exams. 

GIS was a good course as well, and it was well structured with an easy exam in the end. I mostly chose it because it's a very good skill to learn when studying biology.

questions.answer: JCU requires you to be covered by a specific overseas health cover (e.g. OSHC from Allianz Care), which you’ll pay for when you pay your tuition fee when applying for the confirmation of enrolment at the host university.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Vegetables and fruits were cheaper than in Denmark, so a vegetarian diet is quite cheap. Dairy products and alcohol were however quite expensive.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were a lot of student sports - Volleyball, soccer, basket, ultimate frisbee, ect. There were also many BBQs arranged by the university or the dorms.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I think the people who joined a sport were quite happy with it. I didn’t do that however, and I still met a lot of people through my dorm.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
There are really a lot of things to see and visit when in Australia! Townsville in itself might not be the biggest tourist attraction, but if you like to explore nature, then it’s location in the northern Queensland is actually really good. There is first of all a lot of beautiful nature just around the city - e.g. Crystal Creek and Alligator Creek with beautiful waterfalls, rockpools, and streams going through the mountains, and rockslides that you can glide down from. There is also Ross river which runs through Townsville, where small freshwater crocodiles and turtles live in, and you can swim in it by the Pontoon, which is a really nice place to hang out with friends after classes. 

The best place near Townsville however, is Magnetic Island (!!), which is just a 20 minute ferry ride away from the city. The island is very beautiful and nice to walk around on, and you can do many things there - e.g. Do the forts walk and see koalas on the way (the island has the highest concentration of koalas in Australia), and then walk down to Florence bay where you can snorkel on the coral reefs. The visibility varies a lot and is not always great due to Ross river running through Townsville, but it is still really beautiful reefs, where you can see many different corals, fish, sharks, rays, turtles! Me and my friend also got our diving certificate there. We went to Magnetic Island 10 times when we where there, and every time was a pleasure! 

We also did weekend trips to the Whitsundays and Cairns. Cairns is a great place, where you can see a lot of nature - for example the Daintree rainforest, waterfall trips in the tablelands, or diving on the Great Barrier reef!! Me and my two friends did a 3-day liveaboard with the company Prodive, where we lived 3 days on a boat on the Great Barrier with 25 other people and got 11 dives at different diving sites. This was really an amazing experience, and I would definitely recommend it even though it is quite expensive. The Whitsundays is also a very beautiful place know for its white sand beaches and crystal clear water. 

After our semester me and a couple of friends traveled down along the east coast in campervans. This was really nice as it was a very flexible way to travle, and you get to see a lot more, than you would by just traveling with bus from city to city. We “only” traveled along the east coast, and I’m quite happy we focused just on this, as I otherwise would be afraid that the traveling would be kind of superficial.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. It’s very similar to something you already know - mix between english and american.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Live in a dorm, don’t be shy to arrange a dinner/movie night/trip with someone.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Australian people are generally very friendly and helpful. This was really nice, especially when you are in a country so far away from home, where you probably don’t know anyone on beforehand.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1)	Keep an open mind for meeting new people and remember to make an effort and take initiative.
2)	Take all the opportunities you can to travel.
3)	Don't worry too much about your grades - Your subjects are only transferred as pass/fail anyway.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Not anything that i haven't already mentioned.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: All the travelling experiences and the people I’ve met.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Being far away from family and friends, but remember that it’s only for half a year, and time will really fly by so quickly!

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
